title: Vinaya Texts
altTitles: Vinaya Texts (Sacred Books of the East, vols. 13, 17 and 20)
dateDisplay: c. 4th–3rd century BCE; written down in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE
attributionNote: The Vinaya Piṭaka is an anonymous compilation of the Theravada monastic order, traditionally recited at the first council after the Buddha's death. Its rules are presented as the Buddha's own enactments, each occasioned by a case in the community, but the collection took its present shape over generations.
description: The Vinaya Piṭaka is the monastic law of the Theravada canon: the Pātimokkha, the 227 rules recited at the fortnightly assembly, with the narrative that explains each one; the Mahāvagga, on admission to the order, the uposatha, the rains retreat, the closing ceremony, medicines, robes, the kaṭhina, schisms and the duties of teachers; and the Kullavagga, on the minor proceedings, probation and penance, the settlement of disputes, dwellings, the duties of nuns, and the two councils at Rājagaha and Vesālī. It is the fullest surviving picture of early Buddhist monastic life.
historicalContext: The Pali Vinaya was transmitted orally and written down in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE. T. W. Rhys Davids and Hermann Oldenberg translated it in three volumes for the Sacred Books of the East (13, 1881; 17, 1882; 20, 1885). Their work made the monastic law of the Theravada available in English for the first time and remains the standard public-domain translation.
availabilityNote: Complete. All three Sacred Books of the East volumes (13, 17 and 20) are combined here and streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one printed page per chapter. Part I holds the Pātimokkha and the first four Mahāvagga khandhakas; Part II the Fifth to Tenth khandhakas and the first three of the Kullavagga; Part III the Fourth to Twelfth kullavagga khandhakas. Chapter labels carry the khandhaka and the chapter number printed on the page. A page can print two chapters (for example Kullavagga I, chapters 26 and 27); it is labelled with both, and the one page that carries the end of Mahāvagga VIII, chapter 32 together with the opening of Mahāvagga IX says so. The volumes' introductions, notes and indexes are not part of the work.
